title: Copy one array into another array.
shortTitle: Copy one array into another array

s1_definition.profdef: Copying an array creates a new array of the same length and places each source element into the corresponding position of the destination. In Java you can loop manually, or use `System.arraycopy`, `Arrays.copyOf`, or `clone()`. For arrays of objects these produce a shallow copy: the references are duplicated but the objects themselves are shared. It is O(n) time and O(n) space for the new array.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to archive Rajesh's current transaction list before running a risky recalculation. A clerk photocopies the whole list onto a fresh sheet so the original is safe. If the recalculation goes wrong, the archived copy is untouched and can be restored.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make a fresh array of the same size and place each element into it; for objects this copies references, not the objects themselves.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Copying an array creates a new array of the same length and places each source element into the corresponding position of the destination. In Java you can loop manually, or use `System.arraycopy`, `Arrays.copyOf`, or `clone()`. For arrays of objects these produce a shallow copy: the references are duplicated but the objects themselves are shared. It is O(n) time and O(n) space for the new array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants to archive Rajesh's current transaction list before running a risky recalculation. A clerk photocopies the whole list onto a fresh sheet so the original is safe. If the recalculation goes wrong, the archived copy is untouched and can be restored.

**One line to remember:** Make a fresh array of the same size and place each element into it; for objects this copies references, not the objects themselves.

sections.s2_technical:
The clearest way to copy is a manual loop: create `BigDecimal[] dest = new BigDecimal[src.length]` and then `for (int i = 0; i < src.length; i++) dest[i] = src[i];`. This gives you full control and is easy to read.

Java also provides faster built-ins. `System.arraycopy(src, 0, dest, 0, src.length)` is a native method that is usually the fastest. `Arrays.copyOf(src, src.length)` allocates and copies in one call. `src.clone()` also produces a new array with the same contents. All of these produce a shallow copy for object arrays, meaning `dest[i]` points at the same `BigDecimal` object as `src[i]`.

For `BigDecimal` the shallow copy is perfectly safe because `BigDecimal` is immutable: you cannot change the number inside it, you can only create a new one. So even though the copy shares references, nobody can mutate a shared amount. If the elements were mutable objects, like a mutable `Account`, you would need a deep copy, cloning each element, to keep the archive truly independent. Time is O(n) and space is O(n) for the destination.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Before National Bank of India applies an interest recalculation to Rajesh's transaction amounts, it wants a backup of the original list so it can roll back if the recalculation produces wrong figures. The system must copy the array into a separate archive array. This is exactly how array copying works — allocate a new array and place each element in.

Problem 2 — The amounts are BigDecimal, which is immutable, so a shallow copy is safe and cheap. This is exactly why we can use a simple copy here without worrying that a change to the archive would leak back into the original, because nobody can mutate a BigDecimal in place.

The code has an `ArchiveService` class with a `backup` method showing a manual loop, and it also demonstrates `Arrays.copyOf`. The demo backs up Rajesh's amounts, modifies the original, and shows the archive is unaffected.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: original `[1000.00, 2000.00, 3000.00]`.

Step 1 — `backup` allocates a new array of length 3.

Step 2 — The loop copies index 0, 1, 2. The archive is `[1000.00, 2000.00, 3000.00]`, with each slot pointing at the same immutable BigDecimal objects as the original.

Step 3 — The recalculation sets `original[0]` to a brand new BigDecimal `1100.00`. This replaces the reference in the original array only; the archive's slot 0 still points at the old `1000.00` object.

Step 4 — We log both arrays. The original now shows `1100.00` at index 0, but the archive still shows `1000.00`, proving the backup is independent at the slot level.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Archive created: [1000.00, 2000.00, 3000.00]
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Original after recalculation: [1100.00, 2000.00, 3000.00]
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Archive still safe:            [1000.00, 2000.00, 3000.00]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Copying an array means creating a brand new array of the same length and placing each source element into the matching position of the destination. In Java I can do this with a simple loop, or with the built-in helpers like System dot arraycopy, Arrays dot copyOf, or the clone method. All of them run in linear time and allocate a destination of the same size, so the space is linear too.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used array copying to take a backup before a risky interest recalculation. Before the batch job overwrites Rajesh's transaction amounts, I copy the original list into an archive array, so if the recalculation produces wrong figures I can roll back to the archived copy.

The subtle point I always raise is shallow versus deep copy. For an array of objects, these copy operations duplicate the references, not the objects themselves, so both arrays point at the same underlying objects. In my case the elements are BigDecimal, which is immutable, so a shallow copy is completely safe: nobody can change the number inside a BigDecimal, they can only replace a slot with a new BigDecimal, and replacing a slot in one array does not affect the other. If the elements had been mutable objects, I would need a deep copy that clones each element, otherwise a change through one array would be visible through the other, which would defeat the whole purpose of an archive.
